\chapter{La habitación}
\label{ch:es-cuarto}
\hlchaptermodality{455}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can get a room ready and say so: what I have painted and what colour, what to put where, and what to hang out if the sun comes out.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pintar]{pintar — to paint}

\label{lesson:ES-C455-pintar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{verde} and \textbf{arreglar}. One way of fixing a room is to change its colour.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: pintar}
\textbf{pintar} — to paint, both walls and pictures.

\emph{Voy a pintar la cocina de verde} — I'm going to paint the kitchen green. \emph{Recién pintado} — wet paint, the wording on the sign. \emph{¿Quién pintó esto?} — who painted this?

Note the \textbf{de} in \emph{pintar de verde}. Spanish marks the resulting colour with \emph{de}, where English puts the adjective straight after the object.

\textbf{La pintura} is both the paint in the tin and the painting on the wall.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: recién plus a participle}]
\textbf{Recién} means \textquotedblleft{}newly\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}a moment ago\textquotedblright{}, and it attaches only to participles:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sign} & \textbf{what it means} \\
\midrule
\emph{recién pintado} & wet paint \\
\emph{recién llegado} & newly arrived \\
\emph{recién casados} & newlyweds \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

In Spain it never stands alone and never modifies a normal adjective — \emph{recién limpio} is not said. Take it as half of a two-word unit whose other half ends in \emph{-ado} or \emph{-ido}.

Much of Latin America is freer with it. \emph{Recién llegué} — I arrived a moment ago — and \emph{recién ayer} are ordinary in the Southern Cone, where \emph{recién} behaves like a plain adverb of time.

The participle agrees: \emph{recién pintada} for \emph{la pared}, \emph{recién pintados} for \emph{los bancos}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{pingere}, to paint — a verb that also meant to \textbf{embroider}, and behind both of those an older word for \textbf{pricking or cutting a mark} into a surface.

So painting and needlework were one verb in Latin, because both put a design onto cloth. The relatives come off the painting side: English \textbf{picture}, \textbf{pigment}, \textbf{paint} and \textbf{pictorial}, and Spanish \textbf{pintoresco} — worth-painting — which English borrowed through French as \textbf{picturesque}.

The Latin participle \emph{pictus} is where the harder consonants survived: Spanish kept the soft, spoken \emph{pintar} and borrowed the bookish \emph{pictórico} alongside it. Another pair arriving twice, by the two roads.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I'm going to paint the kitchen green
  \item wet paint, as the sign puts it
  \item which preposition goes before the colour
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To paint? (\textbf{Pintar}.) Wet paint? (\textbf{Recién pintado}.) What else did \emph{pingere} mean? (\textbf{To embroider} — both put a design on cloth.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el dormitorio]{el dormitorio — the bedroom}

\label{lesson:ES-C455-dormitorio}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{dormir} and \textbf{el piso}. Name the room in the second where you do the first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el dormitorio}
\textbf{el dormitorio} — the bedroom.

\emph{Un piso de dos dormitorios} — a two-bedroom flat, the wording in every advert. \emph{El dormitorio da al patio} — the bedroom looks onto the courtyard.

\textbf{La habitación} also covers it in speech — \emph{mi habitación} is what a child says — but a property listing counts \emph{dormitorios}, because \emph{habitación} means any room at all.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the vowel that has been breaking all along}]
You met \textbf{duermo} early on, as a verb that changes its stem. It is the same single rule you have now seen in a noun, an adjective and a conjugation:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{plain o} & \textbf{stressed, so ue} \\
\midrule
d\textbf{o}rmir, d\textbf{o}rmitorio & d\textbf{ue}rmo \\
r\textbf{o}dar & la r\textbf{ue}da \\
m\textbf{o}strar & m\textbf{ue}stro \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Dormitorio} keeps the plain \textbf{o} because the stress lands on the \textbf{-to-}, three syllables along. Say \emph{dormitorio} and \emph{duermo} one after the other and you can hear the vowel change as the stress moves.

Nothing here is irregular. One vowel, one condition, and it has been running under the language since the first weeks of it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{dormitorium}, a sleeping place — from \textbf{dormire}, to sleep.

\textbf{-orio} names the place where something is done, and once you have it you can read a lot of signs:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the place for} \\
\midrule
el dormit\textbf{orio} & sleeping \\
el laborat\textbf{orio} & working \\
el velat\textbf{orio} & keeping watch over the dead \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English took \emph{dormitorium} whole as \textbf{dormitory}, and shortened it to \emph{dorm}. It also has \textbf{dormant}, lying asleep, and the \textbf{dormouse}, named for how much of the year it spends doing exactly that.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a two-bedroom flat
  \item I sleep, then the name of the room
  \item why \emph{dormitorio} has no \emph{ue}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The bedroom? (\textbf{El dormitorio}.) What does \emph{-orio} name? (\textbf{The place where something is done}.) Why no \emph{ue}? (\textbf{The stress is elsewhere}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[claro]{claro — light, and clear}

\label{lesson:ES-C455-claro}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{sí, claro} and \textbf{verde}. You have been saying the first for a very long time. This lesson is about what its second word means.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: claro}
\textbf{claro} — light, pale, bright, clear.

\emph{Un dormitorio muy claro} — a very light bedroom, one that gets the sun. \emph{Verde claro} — light green. \emph{Azul claro} — pale blue. The opposite is \textbf{oscuro}, dark.

Beyond colour: \emph{el agua está clara} — the water is clear. \emph{No me queda claro} — I'm not clear about it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the word you have been using without meeting}]
\textbf{Sí, claro} has been in your mouth since early on, as a way of agreeing — \textquotedblleft{}yes, of course\textquotedblright{}. You were told then that it is Latin \emph{clarus}, bright — but never that you could point it at a wall, because the phrase does not need the colour sense to work.

It is the same word. \emph{Claro} on its own means \textbf{it's clear}, and agreeing with somebody by saying \textquotedblleft{}clear!\textquotedblright{} is how Spanish arrives at \textquotedblleft{}of course\textquotedblright{}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you say} & \textbf{what it is doing} \\
\midrule
\emph{sí, claro} & of course — the fixed phrase \\
\emph{un cuarto claro} & a light room — the adjective \\
\emph{claro que sí} & of course — the phrase, emphasised \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This is the fourth time a fixed phrase has turned out to have an ordinary word inside it. \emph{Mira} gave you \emph{mirar}, \emph{el punto} gave \emph{apuntar}, \emph{interesante} gave \emph{interesar}, and now \emph{sí, claro} gives \emph{claro}.

\textbf{Check every new word against the phrases you already say.} By this stage of a language, a surprising share of new vocabulary is not new.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: colour words with claro and oscuro}]
A colour modified by \emph{claro} or \emph{oscuro} \textbf{stops agreeing}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{one thing} & \textbf{more than one} \\
\midrule
\emph{una pared verde} & \emph{unas paredes verd\textbf{es}} \\
\emph{una pared verde claro} & \emph{unas paredes verde claro} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Add the shade and the pair freezes. The reason is that \emph{verde claro} is standing in for \textquotedblleft{}of a light green colour\textquotedblright{} — a description of the shade rather than of the walls — and Spanish leaves such compounds unchanged.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a very light bedroom
  \item light green walls, plural
  \item what \emph{claro} is doing inside \emph{sí, claro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Light, pale? (\textbf{Claro}.) The opposite? (\textbf{Oscuro}.) Does \emph{verde claro} agree in the plural? (\textbf{No} — it freezes.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tender]{tender — hang it out}

\label{lesson:ES-C455-tender}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la tienda} and \textbf{limpio}. A shop is about to turn out to be a stretched thing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tender}
\textbf{tender} — to hang out, to spread, to stretch out.

\emph{Voy a tender la ropa} — I'm going to hang the washing out. \emph{El tendedero} — the airer or the washing line. \emph{Tender la mano} — to hold out your hand.

In a flat with no garden this is daily vocabulary, and the sign in a stairwell saying \emph{no tender ropa en la fachada} is asking you not to hang washing on the front of the building.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: tender is an e-to-ie verb}]
The same break you have watched all chapter, one vowel over:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{stress on the stem} & \textbf{stress on the ending} \\
\midrule
t\textbf{ie}ndo, t\textbf{ie}ndes & tend\textbf{e}mos \\
t\textbf{ie}nde, t\textbf{ie}nden & tend\textbf{é}is \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And now say \textbf{tiendo} and \textbf{la tienda} together. They are the same shape, because \emph{la tienda} \textbf{is} this verb: a shop was a stretched awning, a cloth tent pulled open over a market stall.

The shop chapter named that cloth when it taught \emph{la tienda}; here is the verb it was named from, so the noun and its verb finally sit together. \emph{Tienda de campaña} — a camping tent — kept the original object entirely.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{tendere}, to stretch.

The family in English is long: \textbf{tend}, \textbf{tent}, \textbf{tension}, \textbf{extend}, \textbf{intend}, \textbf{pretend} — to stretch something out in front of you — \textbf{attention}, a stretching towards.

Spanish has the whole set too: \emph{tender}, \emph{la tienda}, \emph{extender}, \emph{pretender}, \emph{la tensión}, \emph{atender}. Every one of them is something being pulled taut, either a cloth or a mind.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I'm going to hang the washing out
  \item I hang out, using the stem-changing form
  \item what a \emph{tienda} originally was
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To hang the washing out? (\textbf{Tender la ropa}.) I hang out? (\textbf{Tiendo}.) What does \emph{tendere} mean? (\textbf{To stretch}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[meter]{meter — put it in}

\label{lesson:ES-C455-meter}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el permiso} and \textbf{la caja}. There is a Latin verb inside the first, and you are about to use it on the second.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: meter}
\textbf{meter} — to put in, to put inside.

\emph{Mete la ropa en la caja} — put the clothes in the box. \emph{Meter la llave} — put the key in. \emph{Se ha metido en la cama} — he's got into bed.

\emph{Meterse} also does the social senses: \emph{no te metas} — don't interfere. \emph{Meterse con alguien} — to pick on somebody.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: meter is not poner}]
Both come out as \textquotedblleft{}put\textquotedblright{} and they are not interchangeable:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you are doing} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
putting something \textbf{inside} something & \textbf{meter} \\
putting something \textbf{somewhere} & \textbf{poner} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Pon el libro en la mesa} — on the table, a surface. \emph{Mete el libro en la caja} — into the box, an inside. Swap them and a Spanish speaker will picture you burying a book in a table.

\emph{Meter} nearly always brings \textbf{en} with it, because \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} is the whole idea of the verb. If there is no inside, you want \emph{poner}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{mittere}, to send — and its participle \emph{missus}.

Spanish wore the plain verb down to \emph{meter} and shifted it from sending to inserting, which is a short move: to send a thing into a box is to put it there. The bookish arrivals kept the shape: \emph{admitir}, \emph{permitir}, \emph{emitir}, \emph{transmitir}.

And there it is in a word you already have. \textbf{El permiso} is \emph{per-} plus \emph{missus}: something \textbf{sent through}. English took the same set as \textbf{permit}, \textbf{admit}, \textbf{mission}, \textbf{missile} and \textbf{message} — every one of them a sending.

So \emph{meter la ropa en la caja} and \emph{pedir permiso} run on one Latin verb, one worn smooth and one carried in from the page.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item put the clothes in the box
  \item put the book on the table, choosing the right verb
  \item what \emph{el permiso} has to do with \emph{meter}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To put inside? (\textbf{Meter}.) Which preposition follows it? (\textbf{En}.) What does \emph{mittere} mean? (\textbf{To send}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(pintar, el dormitorio, claro, tender …]{(pintar, el dormitorio, claro, tender, meter) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R455-repaso-cuarto}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: \emph{to paint}, \emph{the bedroom}, \emph{light}, \emph{to hang out}, \emph{to put in}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the fourth phrase to give up a word}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you already said} & \textbf{the word inside it} \\
\midrule
\emph{interesante} & \textbf{interesar} \\
\emph{mira} & \textbf{mirar} \\
\emph{el punto} & \textbf{apuntar} \\
\emph{sí, claro} & \textbf{claro} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And \textbf{la tienda} joins them from the other direction: a shop turned out to be this chapter's verb, a stretched awning.

\textbf{Claro} is the strongest case yet, because \emph{sí, claro} is among the first things anybody learns to say in Spanish and among the commonest things anybody says. You were told back then that it means \emph{bright} — and still never once used it to describe a room, because agreeing with somebody asks nothing of the colour sense.

The habit to keep: when a new word resembles a phrase you already use, look for the connection before learning it twice.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two verbs that both mean put}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the picture} & \textbf{the verb} \\
\midrule
into an inside & \textbf{meter} — \emph{meter en la caja} \\
onto or at a place & \textbf{poner} — \emph{poner en la mesa} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Meter} comes with \textbf{en} because \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} is the verb's whole meaning. If nothing encloses the thing, \emph{poner} is what you want.

The same test sorts \emph{pintar de verde}, where \textbf{de} marks a resulting colour. Spanish tells you a great deal through its prepositions, and each of these verbs carries one it will not give up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I'm painting the bedroom a light green
  \item put the clothes in the box
  \item which verb you use for a surface
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All five again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence about getting a room ready.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(dejar el piso listo) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C455-sintesis-cuarto}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{pintar} and \textbf{claro}. The message below uses them in the same line, and one of them is not about colour.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
A message between two people sharing a flat. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
Oye, mañana viene mi hermana.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
He \textbf{pintado} el \textbf{dormitorio} de azul \textbf{claro} y huele fuerte, así que deja la ventana abierta.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
¿Puedes \textbf{meter} las cajas del pasillo en el trastero? No me ha dado tiempo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Y si sale el sol, \textbf{tiende} las toallas antes de irte. Gracias.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what colour the bedroom is now, and what to do about the smell
  \item the two jobs being asked for
  \item what has to happen before the towels go out
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{De azul claro} carries both of this chapter's small grammar points at once. \emph{De} marks the resulting colour, and \emph{azul claro} does \textbf{not} agree with anything — no \emph{azules claros} even if there were several walls, because the pair has frozen into a name for the shade.

\textbf{Meter las cajas en el trastero} is \emph{meter} doing exactly its job: a storeroom is an inside, and \emph{poner} would be wrong. Then \textbf{tiende} is the \emph{tú} command of a stem-changing verb, so the \textbf{ie} is there — \emph{tiende}, never \emph{tende}.

Notice the register throughout. \emph{Oye}, \emph{¿puedes…?}, \emph{deja} — every one is \emph{tú}, because this is a flatmate and not a counter. Set it beside the notices in the chapters before this one and the difference is visible in the verb endings alone.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines to a flatmate: say you have painted the bedroom a light colour, ask them to put the boxes in the storeroom, ask them to hang the washing out, and say why.

Then check yourself: did you use \emph{de} before the colour, \emph{meter} for the inside, and the \emph{tú} forms throughout?
\end{tcolorbox}
